dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: You brought back a packet the Nexus could actually use. Now somebody has sent us a display board with one heading for two very different places. The ink has started to glow. We have until the visitors arrive to decide what goes on the two stands.

options.text: I’ll check the royal records first.
I’ll start with the sites marked on the coast map.
I’ll come back.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Door on the left. Follow the register beyond the burial entry. The ink is telling visitors the temple record will take them all the way to the modern catalogue. Check where that trail stops.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Door on the right. The map was folded through the middle. Unfold it before you follow the slips. The coast record asks a different question from the royal one.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The stands stay empty until we can explain both records. The royal room is to the left and the coastal room is to the right. You can leave through the south door and pick this up any time.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Our spare Lens and Thread are on the desk. Take what is missing from your kit. You can keep them if you need to return to the Nexus.

options.text: Take the Date-Kind Lens.
Take the Provenance Thread.
Leave the desk.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The Lens separates a date for a building from the date of a later account.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Carry the Thread to the first marker. It will leave a space where we have a gap.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: The name can stay on the label with its basis. You left the missing transfer open. Someone can bring us another record later without having to start the case over.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: One visitor saw the same name twice and asked why we need two records. Take the Lens to the temple sheet and the catalogue. The Thread begins at the burial marker. When you reach the end, give the stand a heading you can defend.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: Pull the site map flat. Then follow the three slips and read the context file. The old heading makes every burial here sound as if it followed the same practice. The file gives us reasons to be more careful.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: Now we can show why context matters. A map puts readers in the right place, and the context file tells them what preservation can and cannot show on its own.

options.text: Leave the site map uppermost.
Leave the context file open at the preservation notes.
I’ll leave the order for later.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: The next reader makes for the map first. A second slip sends them to the preservation notes once they find the site.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: Two readers stop over the preservation notes and notice the different conditions. One turns over the folder and finds the map.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: We can open the display with two separate record stands, put a comparison slip between them, or open the inquiry desk while the cases wait. The gap in the royal file and the limits of the coastal record stay on the page in all three.

options.text: Open two stands. Give each record room.
Put a comparison slip between the two stands.
Hold the cases for review. Open the inquiry desk today.
I’ll look through the rooms again.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The room opens with a stand for each place. A reader stops at the gap in the royal chain. At the second stand, another asks whether preservation by itself can tell us how a burial was treated. The desk keeper is taking both requests.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Visitors walk from the comparison slip to the two records and back. A reader points to the column marked 'what we can follow' and asks where the trail goes thin in each case. The desk keeper has pulled up a chair.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The cases stay closed. The evidence desk opens. Visitors can ask why the heading was withheld and view the two record summaries while the stands wait. A reader asks where to look for the missing link.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The inquiry desk is open to the east. If you need to catch the portal, use the south door. The two rooms stay open if you want to check a record again.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader copied the royal heading at the first stand. They want to check the missing link when they get home. Another read only the coastal stand. They asked where we recorded its scope. How should we leave the next reader a route to the two records?

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A visitor copied our comparison slip. Their friend took that single page to mean the two cases shared a history. Both want to know which record supports each line. How shall we keep the explanation with its source?

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A visitor thinks a closed case means we have no usable records. We can leave a trace of what is known and where the gap remains while the display waits. Where should that trace live?

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A desk copy can hold the whole reference trail. Short notes at each record can travel with a quick copy. This room has time to prepare one first.

options.text: File a traceable copy at the inquiry desk.
Clip the limits and references to the relevant records.
Leave the request open.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader opens the desk copy and follows the two references in order. At the Nexus, a second copy will sit beside the return door for people who miss this room.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader takes away a reference slip with the gap still marked. The next copy is going to the Nexus, where someone can find it beside the return door.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A proof sheet for the excavation case has a date, a doorway and an empty space where the workers’ names could go. A first journal entry, a later study and the archive’s account of the workforce have arrived. We can put one claim at the top, with the other records below.

options.text: Lead with the named foremen. Leave other names open.
Lead with a dated trail from the journal to the later note.
Leave the proof on the desk.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: The foremen’s names have room on the proof. A reader asks whose names the archive did not keep. The dated documents are below the heading, with spaces for what they cannot settle.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: The note sits later on the trail than the journal. A reader points to the gap between when a record was made and when its subject happened. The workforce record stays next to the dates, with the four names in view.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: A returning visitor remembers starting at the temple picture. Another says their guide began with the burial file. Their memories help us find where each tour began. The sources still carry their own dates. Try the start clip in both positions before we open the doors.

options.text: Slide the start clip to the reign and temple.
Slide the start clip to the burial.
Choose a starting card for the visitors.
Read the temple-first route again.
Read the burial-first route again.
Leave the start clip here.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: With the temple first, the trail opens at a place the king built for remembrance. The Ministry gives Ramesses II’s reign as about 1279–1213 BCE. Keep that range beside ‘reign’. A visitor just asked which of those years the temple went up. The site record here gives a reign, and the trail can continue to a separate burial file.

options.text: Slide the start clip to the burial.
Choose a starting card for the visitors.
Leave the clip by the temple.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: With the burial first, a visitor can start the custody trail at KV 7. The next place listed on the museum copy is the later cache at Deir el-Bahari. Leave the move date blank. The Ramesseum stays on the side flap for the earlier reign. A reader trying to follow the later move can carry that smaller trail.

options.text: Slide the start clip to the reign and temple.
Choose a starting card for the visitors.
Leave the clip by the burial file.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: We can start a walk through a reign and its place of remembrance, or open the trail at its first recorded burial place. The starting card guides the questions people bring to the rest. Keep the other file in reach and its dates on its own line.

options.text: Open with the temple during the reign. Keep the custody trail on its own tab.
Open with the burial and later safekeeping. Keep the temple on the earlier tab.
Leave the two starting cards beside the clip.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: A visitor points to the temple card by the Cold Store’s doorway and asks how the king planned to be remembered. The side tab can still lead them to the later custody record. The approximate reign dates stay with the Ministry’s site record.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader at the burial-first card follows the known places and points to the blank move date. They ask who could speak for that handover. The museum file names the custody places. Who authorised the move remains a separate question.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I took the late slot. A reader at the rail asked me which line I’d signed. Turns out it was useful to have one I could point to. Now my trainee needs credit for the next delivery. They asked to keep their name off the wall.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I made the first slot. The receiver lifted the fold and asked about Leila’s clips. Nobody at the wall did. Now my trainee needs credit for a delivery. They asked to check it in at the desk.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I took their slip. The receiver thought I’d checked the file, so we had to sit down again. I logged the delivery on its own. My trainee made the next run and asked to keep their name off the wall.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: A visitor wants a row of names for the workers in the excavation account. Take our form down to the trays by the archive acknowledgments. I’ll meet you back here. The dispatch rail and the Review Room use the same clips for very different records.

options.text: Unfold the carrier copy from the Nile Archive.
Ask Nellis for the receiving desk’s copy.
I’ll leave the trays for now.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: Here is the arrival you signed for, and here is Leila’s line about the papyrus. Put it on the right-hand tray with the current roster. The older acknowledgments go on the left.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I made a second line here when the receiver asked. Take this version of the receipt to the right-hand tray. The older acknowledgments go on the left.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: The receiving roster is beside me. The Review Room holds the real excavation acknowledgments. Once the first main display goes up, we can use both trays down there.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The left tray takes the excavation acknowledgments. Carter named four Egyptian foremen; other workers appear in photographs. The collection has no diaries or letters written by those workers. The right tray takes a delivery receipt and the trainee’s request to keep their name at the desk.

options.text: Clip the excavation source and current roster to separate trays.
Leave the trays on the shelf.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The left tray credits the four foremen the archive can identify. Its spare clip asks what source could add a name. The right tray records the trainee’s shift without carrying their name to the wall. Pick up both trays and take them back to Nellis.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: The trainee can get credit either way. On the rail, readers can see where the old acknowledgments stop and bring a source. At the desk, a keeper can talk it through and check a proposed name with them. They have to catch us when we’re here.

options.text: Pin the source and its open question on the public rail.
Open a source check at the staffed desk.
Leave Nellis the receipt and decline the review shift.
Let me think by the trays.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: A visitor follows the line to the excavation account and sees where the named list ends. I can take this board to the next open shift. I’ve filed the trainee’s name at the desk, where they asked me to keep it.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I’ll be at the low bench after receiving. A visitor can bring a source and I can hear them out before a name goes up. The rail tells them when to come. The trainee’s shift is logged.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: Fair. I can log the arrival now. I’ll leave the clip open for a source and keep the trainee’s receipt at the desk. The next keeper can choose a review shift.

dialogue.speaker: handoff-nellis
dialogue.text: I have a signed arrival for the trainee. The display can still change when someone brings another source. Check the rail or the low bench before you go.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: A shallow rim can make a paper practice basket look different from one side. Try this paper version on its edge and on a base cradle. Hold the paper and table fixed. Mikaela’s own work stays with the museum case and her name.

options.text: Rest the same practice model on its narrow edge and tap the board once.
Set the practice model flat on the base cradle and tap the board once.
Leave the paper model on the mat.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: The paper rim bends against the edge. Go to the side mark and check where it meets the bench. The old catalogue entry still speaks for the object in Melbourne.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: The base stayed flat and the rim stood clear. Go to the side mark. You can see the space under the rim without leaning on it.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The apprentice wants to see the open shape and how the maker learned it. The carrier needs room to move the practice model after the hall closes. A low cradle leaves the rim clear. A side-view sheet can sit out while the model waits on its support. Both dates can stay with Mikaela’s name.

options.text: Put the level practice cradle where the apprentice can see its opening.
Hang the side view and keep the model on its supported shelf.
Leave the mat and source tabs ready.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The apprentice can walk around the opening. The underside has its own drawing at the source. Check that the name and both dates stay clear beside the rim.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: A visitor can compare width and depth without moving a model. The carrier can come to the shelf for the practice shape after closing. Check that the side-view panel still carries Mikaela’s name.

missions.title: The Missing Transfer
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How can a public record name what it knows and still leave room for a missing link?
missions.stake: If the gap in the file is hidden, a family loses its claim to an ancestor's name.

objectives.title: Hear the registrar’s plan for the two stands.
Trace the royal catalogue and repair the heading in the royal room.
Compare the site map and context file in the coastal room.
Return to the registrar and decide how to open the display.

missions.title: Room for a Reply
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What helps a reader check a claim after it leaves the room?

objectives.title: Take the reader’s request at the inquiry desk.

missions.title: Names on the Proof
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What can the date and author of a record tell us about whose story survives?

objectives.title: Inspect the excavation files and use the Lens on the journal and the later note.
Put a lead on the excavation proof sheet.

missions.title: Where the File Begins
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How does choosing a starting point change what a historical display helps visitors investigate?

objectives.title: Try two starting points on the Royal Records clip.
Open one public route while leaving the other source in reach.

missions.title: A Place for the Next Name
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How can a display recognise work and give readers a way to check new names?

objectives.title: Set the old acknowledgments and new receiving roster on separate trays.
Choose how the Cold Store handles the name request and check the result.

missions.title: The Open Rim
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How does the way we show an object change what a visitor can see about its maker?

objectives.title: Read Mikaela’s basket record and two separate catalogue date fields.
Compare two supports on the same paper model.
Set out a useful view and check that both date fields and the maker’s name remain.

threads.title: The custody trail

nodes.label: Burial record
nodes.text: Pin the burial reference from the catalogue. The temple sheet can help place the reign. It cannot follow the later moves.

nodes.label: A later location
nodes.text: Thread the record toward Deir el-Bahari. The summary gives a later place, with room between the two entries.

nodes.label: Museum catalogue
nodes.text: The museum uses the attribution Ramesses II. Keep its name with the custody history and the catalogue that reports it.

gap.text: No transfer slip fills this space in the copy we have. Leave it open without tearing either endpoint off the line.

threads.limit: These stops follow a museum summary. We have not independently verified each transfer.

threads.title: The site and context trail

nodes.label: The site map
nodes.text: Start with the places registered in the map. A label for one coast still needs a named site.

nodes.label: Conditions and practice
nodes.text: Follow the slip to the context file. The record describes more than one way preservation could occur. Check which process the record can actually support.

nodes.label: The evidence in place
nodes.text: Clip the site and the file together. Similar preservation can leave very different histories behind it.

gap.text: This file cannot recover a particular person's wishes or every detail of a burial.

threads.limit: Comparison starts with the evidence at each place. A resemblance cannot establish a shared practice.

labelKits.title: The royal records heading
labelKits.oldLabel: A NAME PROVED BY THE TEMPLE

legends.subject: Record to put first
legends.limit: Note to keep beside the heading
legends.intro: The proof still says the temple settles the whole trail. Pin a heading to a record that can carry it. You can leave a note where the trail goes quiet.

subjects.text: The museum's record for Ramesses II

criteria.text: A monument linked to the reign
A name with a reported custody history
The temple proves every link in the custody chain

limits.text: Some transfer steps are missing from this record.
The temple and the later catalogue tell different parts of the story.

supports.subject: temple
supports.heard: A visitor follows the heading to the temple sheet and asks where the later records begin.

supports.subject: catalogue
supports.heard: The reader keeps the museum attribution beside the known locations and the missing transfer.

supports.subject: temple
supports.weak: A visitor traces a straight line from the temple sheet to the catalogue. There is no transfer record in the space where the line crosses.

weak.noSupport: The gold lights up the space where the heading needs a record.
weak.tooStrong: A reader follows the title farther than the record can take them. The gold catches on the missing link.

hints.text: Someone has set out two empty stands in the Cold Store.
The desk faces the two north doors.
Speak to Registrar Aster in the middle of the hall.
At the desk, take either starting route. The other room stays open.
A building and a museum file can have the same name on them.
Look for the temple sheet and the custody file in the left room.
After inspecting them, follow the Thread from the burial marker to the catalogue marker.
At the heading stand, use the temple record for a monument claim or the museum record for the custody claim.
Start by finding out which coast the file describes.
The right room has a map and a context file.
Inspect both. Follow the site marker, conditions marker and context marker in that order.
Keep the two preservation contexts separate. You can show either record first when the keeper asks.
Both rooms leave something a visitor can check.
Use the passage back to the Cold Store after following both trails.
Speak to Aster. The space between the stands can hold a comparison, or they can stand apart.
Choose separate records, a paired display, or an open review desk with the cases held.
Someone is asking where the heading came from.
Go to the inquiry room east of the Cold Store.
Talk to the keeper by the desk and listen to the visitor’s request.
Leave a full reference copy at the desk or clip individual references to the relevant records.
The inquiry room holds another set of records.
Find the journal, the later note, and the account of the workforce.
Inspect all three. Put the Lens on the journal and the later note.
The Lens shows when each record was made. It leaves earlier events open.
The heading at the top catches the eye first.
Read the proof sheet near the files.
Choose which part of the record visitors should see first.
The names can lead, or the two dated documents can lead. The other record stays on the proof.
The two source dates describe different things.
Use the Date-Kind Lens at the Ramesseum site record and the royal custody file.
Find the movable start clip in the Royal Records room after reading both cases.
Try the clip with the reign and temple first, then with the burial first. Check which claims each opens.
A starting card gives a reader a question to follow.
Consider a reader asking about remembrance and one tracing a later move.
At the Royal Records clip choose a public start after trying both previews.
Put the temple card in the Cold Store or start the custody trail at the burial. The other record stays in reach.
Nellis has reached the Cold Store and remembers the Nile receipt.
Meet Nellis beside the Cold Store’s receiving roster. Show them your copy or ask for theirs.
Read the trainee’s permission by the roster and the excavation acknowledgments in the Review Room.
The Review Room opens after the first main display. Clip both records to their own trays below the workforce case.
A visitor wants to add names to the display.
Return to Nellis after clipping both records to their trays.
Choose a public source question, a staffed desk, or leave the review open with Nellis.
Look at the result on the rail or low bench. The trainee’s name stays at the desk on every route.
A maker’s name and two dates belong to a shallow basket in the Cold Store.
Find Mikaela Rose Cottingham’s binak by the material shelf.
Read the loose slip that distinguishes the catalogue heading from Date Made.
Keep both fields with X 104841. The paper trial belongs to this archive.
There is a paper model near the catalogue.
Try the narrow edge and then the base cradle on the same board.
Read the side mark after each move.
Compare what the paper rim does under the same tap.
An apprentice and a carrier need different views.
Take the two support results to Aster’s stand.
Put the level cradle where someone can see it or hang the side view.
Check the outcome. Its paired tabs give the source and the job separate lines.

journal.text: The temple sheet and custody file carry different claims. The Thread left room for a transfer we could not follow.
The sites and conditions made a difference to what we could infer from the coastal record.
We opened the room with a way to check each record. The same evidence can meet different readers in different forms.
We left a route from the public display to the record that could support it.

journal.title: Where the file begins
journal.text: Two visitors remembered different first stops in the room. I checked the site record and the custody account, then chose which would open the trail. The reign range stayed with the temple record and the unknown move date stayed open.

The Nile packet taught us to give receipt and review their own lines. The excavation acknowledgments name four foremen. The new delivery roster has its own purpose and permission. The space for another supported name stays open.

moments.did: Left a route to the records for readers who missed the display.
moments.prompt: Whose route to the record changed because of what you left?

moments.did: You kept a trainee’s work on the receiving roster and left room for someone to check the historical display.
moments.prompt: Who could bring a source to the next check, and how would they find the keeper?

moments.did: You chose a readable view and left Mikaela’s name beside the two catalogue fields.
moments.prompt: What would a visitor miss if only the object’s shape were on the stand?

chronicle.title: The runner carried two records
chronicle.text: Nellis remembered the Nile packet. A trainee’s delivery was credited with their name kept at the desk. The excavation display still has room for another source.

sources.title: Museums Victoria, Binak by Mikaela Rose Cottingham, X 104841
sources.locator: Object summary, First Peoples fields, association Date Made, dimensions and image rights
sources.supports: The record attributes this grass-fibre coiled bundle basket to Wurundjeri creator Mikaela Rose Cottingham. It describes her learning coil weaving at Bunjilaka and lists a shallow form. The heading and First Peoples field say 2012, while the Date Made association says 2011.

cards.title: Mikaela Rose Cottingham’s binak, X 104841
cards.text: Museums Victoria records a shallow basket made by Mikaela Rose Cottingham, who is Wurundjeri. She learned coil weaving through work for an exhibition at Melbourne Museum and by studying historical baskets. This binak uses bundles of grass fibre.
cards.limits: The heading and First Peoples date show 2012. The associated Date Made field shows 2011. This record leaves the exact year open. The Cold Store diagram is a generic teaching outline.

exhibits.name: Mikaela Rose Cottingham’s binak
exhibits.dateText: 2011 in Date Made, 2012 in the catalogue heading.
exhibits.dateKind: Two dates printed in fields of the same museum record.
exhibits.summary: Museums Victoria X 104841 is a shallow grass-fibre basket made with coiled bundles. The maker learned and experimented with the form while taking part in an exhibition project.
exhibits.altText: An original pixel schematic of a shallow basket profile and its supporting board. The outline illustrates the teaching model.

items.name: Paired context tabs
items.description: One tab keeps a name with its source. The other holds the action someone needs to take. Seagrass Steps has a place for both on its map rail.
